text: Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place where gold is refined.
Iron is taken from the dust, and copper is smelted from stone.
Man puts an end to the darkness; he searches to the farthest limit for ore in gloom and deep shadow.
He sinks a shaft far from where anyone lives, in places forgotten by the foot of man; there the miners dangle and sway, far from human company.

versions.text: He sinks a shaft far from where anyone lives, in places forgotten by the foot of man; there he dangles and sways, far from human company.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verbs דַּלּוּ ... נָעוּ are plural, referring to the miners collectively, while the opening verb פָּרַץ is singular. Rendering the second clause with a plural subject preserves the shift and avoids the slightly odd image of a single unnamed 'he' dangling.

text: As for the earth, out of it comes food, yet underneath it is turned up as by fire.

versions.text: The earth, from which food comes, is turned over below as if by fire.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew sets up a contrast between the earth's surface, which yields bread, and what lies beneath it, which is upheaved as by fire. The current relative-clause construction blurs that contrast and reads awkwardly aloud.

text: Its stones are the place of sapphires, and its dust holds gold.
No bird of prey knows that path; no falcon's eye has seen it.
The proud beasts have not trodden it; no lion has passed that way.
Man lays his hand on the flinty rock and overturns mountains at their roots.
He cuts channels through the rock, and his eye sees every precious thing.
He dams up the sources of the streams and brings hidden things to light.
But where can wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?
No one knows its worth, and it is not found in the land of the living.
The deep says, "It is not in me"; the sea says, "It is not with me."
It cannot be bought with gold, nor can its price be weighed out in silver.
It cannot be valued against the gold of Ophir, against precious onyx or sapphire.
Neither gold nor crystal can equal it, nor can it be exchanged for vessels of fine gold.
Coral and quartz are not worth mentioning; the price of wisdom is beyond pearls.
The topaz of Cush cannot equal it, nor can it be valued against pure gold.
From where, then, does wisdom come? And where is the place of understanding?
It is hidden from the eyes of every living thing, concealed even from the birds of the sky.
Abaddon and Death say, "We have only heard a report of it with our ears."

versions.text: Destruction and Death say, "We have heard a rumor of it with our ears."
versions.explanation: אֲבַדּוֹן is a proper name for the realm of the dead here, parallel to Death and the Deep and Sea in verse 14; 'Destruction' loses that personified sense. Adding 'only' also brings out the contrast with God's full knowledge in the following verse. A footnote could explain that Abaddon means 'place of destruction,' the realm of the dead.

text: God understands the way to it, and he knows its place.
For he looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.
When he gave the wind its weight and measured out the waters,
when he set a decree for the rain and a path for the thunderbolt,
then he saw wisdom and declared it; he established it and searched it out.
And he said to man, "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding."
